description: We are Antoshka, a team of students passionate about technology and space. Our goal is to create a fun, interactive astronaut training game using AI and simulations. We love coding, solving problems, and bringing creative ideas to life. Join us and let's inspire future astronauts!
summary: NASAFormation is a first-person 3D Mars outpost game for kids aged 7–12, made in Godot by Team Antoshka from Uzbekistan. Players land at the UZ-01 capsule, mine and craft, then build power, habitats and machines. The core lesson is that power is finite. In Outpost Control, radiation shielding (0.80 kW), food grow lights (0.90 kW) and an Earth radio (0.55 kW) draw on one supply. When a dust storm cuts solar output, as in our test with 1.17 kW generated against 2.75 kW requested, some systems have to wait. The Storm Salvage mission asks players to keep only one system alive on a 1.05 kW reserve, and the journal records what happened. Oxygen, water and food meters, a radiation risk meter and a modelled Earth signal delay make every choice count. Real NASA facts and imagery, such as Mars Trek elevation maps, a Curiosity sunset, sol length and radiation measurements, are cited inside the game, so players learn where these constraints come from.
details:
NASAFormation turns the challenge's engineering trade-offs into a playable Mars mission for kids aged 7–12. The player is the astronaut of the Uzbekistan UZ-01 lander. A narrated, captioned Mission Control intro and a visor showing the next five objectives teach the basics: walk, mine, craft an oxygen capsule, build a wind turbine and a pressure drill, then a habitat. After that, the player has to keep the crew alive while the outpost grows.

How it works
- Life support: suit oxygen, water and food run down over time. The landing pod and sealed habitats refill oxygen, even during a power outage.
- Power budget: every machine has a power rating. A wind turbine makes 1.2 kW and a T1 solar array 6.5 kW, while drills, heaters and growers use power. The Outpost Control panel (P) gives shelter shielding (0.80 kW), food grow lights (0.90 kW) and the Earth radio (0.55 kW) priority over other machines and shows generated against requested kilowatts.
- Space weather: dust storms cut solar output, and solar storms raise radiation exposure. In the game model, exposure inside a shelter with powered shielding is about 11% of the outdoor rate, against 48% in an unshielded shelter.
- Communication delay: the radio sends a report, and the reply arrives after a modelled 14-minute one-way delay, compressed by the game clock.
- Storm Salvage: the player recovers a circuit board from a wreck, installs it, then at storm peak routes a 1.05 kW reserve to only one system for 75 seconds. The journal records the result, for example "Shelter shielding stayed powered. Food and radio waited."
- Expedition planner (M): estimates the round-trip oxygen to a waypoint and lists the nearest shelters and the next dust and solar storm windows.
- Progression: a Terraform Index built from pressure, heat, oxygen and biomass unlocks better machines over six stages and nine visual milestones, ending with an Earth-return vehicle. Terraforming, rain and plants are labelled in the game as speculative fiction, not present-day Mars.

Grounding in NASA science
The in-game "Mars science & data" panel explains each rule in plain words and links to its NASA source. The orbital atlas shows real NASA/JPL Mars Trek elevation tiles and a Curiosity Mastcam sunset. Storms follow a generated schedule and are never presented as live data.

Benefits
Costs and power draw are always visible, so kids see why a choice matters. They face consequences rather than quiz questions, and storms make each playthrough a little different. The game runs fully offline, which suits classrooms with weak internet. Relaxed, Standard and Challenge difficulty let younger players learn without harsh failure.

What we hope to achieve
We want players to leave understanding three real constraints: power is limited, shelter plus shielding lowers radiation exposure, and Earth cannot answer instantly. Next, we plan to bring in real NASA DONKI space-weather events and RadLab dose data, add a simpler kid mode, build a browser version and playtest with children and teachers.

Tools
Godot Engine 4.4.1 (GL Compatibility renderer), about 7,650 lines of GDScript in 14 scripts, Godot shaders for terrain, sky and water, procedural 3D models, a Node.js script that generates our original music, Windows text-to-speech (Microsoft Hazel) for Mission Control, and a small C# Windows launcher. The Windows build bundles the Godot runtime and needs no installation.

Testing and limitations
On 15 November 2026 we ran the game's built-in tests from source with Godot 4.4.1 for macOS. The logic self-test passed 79 of 79 checks and the rendered test passed 125 of 126; the one failure was the Basalt Lava Tube walk-in passage check. Limitations: Windows download only, with no browser build yet; the 3D controls may be hard for the youngest players, and we have not playtested with children; there are no live NASA feeds; and frame rate is below our 60 FPS target on integrated graphics (we measured 31–47 FPS).
